overview: Achelousaurus was a centrosaurine ceratopsid from Late Cretaceous Montana, named for the shape-changing Greek river deity Achelous. It had a thickened nasal boss rather than a long nasal horn, placing it among the unusual short-frilled ceratopsids close to Pachyrhinosaurus.

The genus is known from a small number of skull-dominated specimens from the Two Medicine Formation. Its anatomy is important because it may document part of an evolutionary sequence among centrosaurines in Montana, linking horned forms such as Einiosaurus with the boss-nosed condition seen in Pachyrhinosaurus.

fossilSites.name: Two Medicine Formation
fossilSites.note: Campanian deposits preserving Achelousaurus and other centrosaurine ceratopsids.

articles.title: Why it matters
articles.body: Achelousaurus is useful for studying horn and nasal-boss evolution in centrosaurines, one of the most visually specialised ceratopsid lineages.

articles.title: Evidence limit
articles.body: Few dated occurrences are recorded, so claims about range, abundance or variation within the genus are not well supported.

record.description: Achelousaurus horneri was a centrosaurine ceratopsid from the upper Two Medicine Formation of Montana. Several skulls and less complete postcranial remains show adults with roughened nasal and brow bosses rather than long horns.
facts: The sample includes three relatively complete adult skulls plus younger individuals.
The proposed evolutionary sequence involving Einiosaurus and Pachyrhinosaurus remains a phylogenetic interpretation, not a directly observed lineage.

review.ageReviewNote: Type-locality evidence places the genus in the late Campanian upper Two Medicine Formation.
